03 · Exploratory data analysis¶

CSE273 Unit III. Types of data, loading and first inspection, univariate and bivariate analysis, correlation and multicollinearity, skewness and kurtosis, patterns, anomalies and trends, and how EDA feeds the modelling work.

EDA is where most of the useful decisions get made. The question for this dataset: what actually drives irrigation need, and is anything in the data going to cause trouble for a model?

In [1]:
try:
    import groundwork
except ImportError:  # running on Kaggle
    %pip install -q git+https://github.com/LuShadowX/Groundwork
    import groundwork

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
from groundwork import data, plotting
plotting.setup()
PALETTE = plotting.CLASS_COLORS

1. Types of data¶

Kind Sub-type Columns here
Quantitative continuous soil pH, moisture, organic carbon, conductivity, temperature, humidity, rainfall, sunlight, wind, field area, previous irrigation
discrete (none; id is a counter, not a measurement)
Qualitative nominal (no order) soil type, crop type, season, irrigation type, water source, region, mulching
ordinal (ordered) crop growth stage (Sowing → Vegetative → Flowering → Harvest), and the target Low < Medium < High

The type decides the tools: means and histograms for quantitative columns, counts and bar charts for qualitative ones, and a different encoding for nominal vs ordinal in CSE274.

3. Univariate analysis¶

A. Histogram (numerical)¶

In [4]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 4, figsize=(13, 8))
for ax, col in zip(axes.flat, num):
    ax.hist(df[col], bins=50, color=plotting.ACCENT, alpha=0.85)
    ax.set_title(col.replace("_", " "), fontsize=10)
    ax.set_yticks([])
axes.flat[-1].axis("off")
fig.suptitle("Distribution of every numeric feature", fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout()
plotting.save("g03-histograms")
plt.show()

Most features are close to uniform (flat between a minimum and a maximum), typical of synthetic Playground data. Rainfall is the only one with a visible hump in the middle and thinner ends.

B. Box plot (numerical)¶

In [5]:
s = data.sample(30_000, seed=3)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13, 4))
for ax, col in zip(axes, ["Soil_Moisture", "Temperature_C", "Rainfall_mm", "Wind_Speed_kmh"]):
    sns.boxplot(data=s, x=data.TARGET, y=col, hue=data.TARGET, palette=PALETTE, ax=ax, legend=False, fliersize=1)
    ax.set_xlabel("")
fig.suptitle("The four features that move with irrigation need", fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout()
plotting.save("g03-boxplots")
plt.show()

C. Count plots (categorical)¶

In [6]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(14, 6.5))
for ax, col in zip(axes.flat, cat):
    order = df[col].value_counts().index
    sns.countplot(data=s, x=col, hue=data.TARGET, palette=PALETTE, order=order, ax=ax, legend=False)
    ax.set_title(col.replace("_", " "), fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("")
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=30, labelsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
plotting.save("g03-countplots")
plt.show()

Two categorical features stand out: growth stage (High is almost absent at Sowing and Harvest) and mulching (mulched fields rarely need a lot of water). The rest look evenly spread.

4. Bivariate analysis¶

A. Scatter plot (numerical vs numerical)¶

In [7]:
g = sns.jointplot(data=s.sample(8000, random_state=0), x="Soil_Moisture", y="Temperature_C", hue=data.TARGET,
                  palette=PALETTE, s=10, alpha=0.5, height=6)
g.figure.suptitle("Moisture against temperature", y=1.02, fontweight="bold")
plotting.save("g03-joint", g.figure)
plt.show()

B. Line plot (numerical vs sequential)¶

The data has no dates, but rainfall can be treated as an ordered axis: mean need score (Low = 0, Medium = 1, High = 2) across rainfall deciles, one line per growth stage.

In [8]:
s2 = df.assign(need=df[data.TARGET].cat.codes, rain_decile=pd.qcut(df["Rainfall_mm"], 10, labels=False) + 1)
line = s2.groupby(["rain_decile", "Crop_Growth_Stage"])["need"].mean().unstack()
ax = line.plot(marker="o")
ax.set(xlabel="rainfall decile (1 = driest)", ylabel="mean need score", title="Rainfall only matters for the driest 10% of fields")
plotting.save("g03-line")
plt.show()

Two things show up: the vegetative and flowering stages sit far above sowing and harvest at every rainfall level, and rainfall itself only matters at the dry end. Need jumps in the driest decile and is flat everywhere else, which is a threshold effect rather than a straight-line one (trees handle that; a linear model would miss it).

C. Violin plot (categorical vs numerical)¶

In [9]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.5))
sns.violinplot(data=s, x="Crop_Growth_Stage", y="Soil_Moisture", hue=data.TARGET, palette=PALETTE,
               order=["Sowing", "Vegetative", "Flowering", "Harvest"], cut=0, inner="quartile", ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Soil moisture by growth stage and need")
plotting.save("g03-violin")

B. Multicollinearity¶

Features that are strongly correlated with each other make linear-model coefficients unstable. The variance inflation factor, VIF = 1 / (1 − R²) where R² comes from regressing a feature on all the others, measures it. VIF above 5–10 is a warning.

In [12]:
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor
from statsmodels.tools.tools import add_constant

Xv = add_constant(s[num])
vif = pd.Series([variance_inflation_factor(Xv.values, i) for i in range(1, Xv.shape[1])], index=num, name="VIF")
print(vif.round(3).sort_values(ascending=False))

# a deliberately collinear feature, to see what VIF does when there is a problem
Xc = s[num].assign(Moisture_copy=s["Soil_Moisture"] * 0.9 + np.random.default_rng(0).normal(0, 1, len(s)))
Xc = add_constant(Xc)
print("\nwith a near-copy of soil moisture added:")
print(pd.Series([variance_inflation_factor(Xc.values, i) for i in range(1, Xc.shape[1])], index=Xc.columns[1:]).round(1).loc[["Soil_Moisture", "Moisture_copy"]])

Soil_Moisture              1.006
Rainfall_mm                1.005
Temperature_C              1.003
Wind_Speed_kmh             1.003
Organic_Carbon             1.002
Previous_Irrigation_mm     1.002
Electrical_Conductivity    1.001
Humidity                   1.001
Sunlight_Hours             1.001

with a near-copy of soil moisture added:
Soil_Moisture    219.3
Moisture_copy    219.3
dtype: float64

All real features have VIF ≈ 1: they are independent of each other, so there is no multicollinearity to fix. The added near-copy shows what a problem looks like (VIF in the hundreds).

6. Distribution analysis¶

A. Skewness and B. kurtosis¶

Skewness measures asymmetry (0 for a symmetric distribution, negative = long left tail). Excess kurtosis measures tail weight relative to a normal distribution (0 = normal, negative = lighter tails / flatter, like a uniform's −1.2).

In [13]:
shape = pd.DataFrame({
    "skewness": df[num].skew(),
    "excess kurtosis": df[num].kurt(),
}).round(3)
shape["looks like"] = np.select(
    [shape["excess kurtosis"] < -1.0, shape["skewness"].abs() > 0.5], ["uniform-ish (flat)", "skewed"], "roughly symmetric")
shape.sort_values("skewness")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.6))
for ax, col in zip(axes, ["Rainfall_mm", "Soil_Moisture", "Organic_Carbon"]):
    x = df[col]
    ax.hist(x, bins=60, density=True, color=plotting.ACCENT, alpha=0.7)
    grid = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), 200)
    ax.plot(grid, stats.norm.pdf(grid, x.mean(), x.std()), color="#e76f51", lw=2, label="normal with same mean, sd")
    ax.set_title(f"{col}\nskew {x.skew():.2f} · kurtosis {x.kurt():.2f}", fontsize=10)
    ax.set_yticks([])
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
plotting.save("g03-skew")
plt.show()

7. Detecting patterns, anomalies and trends¶

A. Patterns¶

The strongest pattern is an interaction: mulching cuts the High share sharply, but only in the stages where crops need water.

In [15]:
pat = (df.groupby(["Crop_Growth_Stage", "Mulching_Used"])[data.TARGET]
         .apply(lambda t: (t == "High").mean()).unstack().loc[["Sowing", "Vegetative", "Flowering", "Harvest"]])
ax = pat.plot.bar(rot=0, color=["#e76f51", "#2a9d8f"])
ax.set(ylabel="share of High fields", title="Mulching matters in the vegetative and flowering stages")
plotting.save("g03-pattern")
plt.show()
pat.round(3)

B. Anomalies (outliers)¶

Two standard rules: values more than 1.5 IQR outside the quartiles, and |z| > 3.

In [16]:
def outlier_table(frame):
    q1, q3 = frame[num].quantile(0.25), frame[num].quantile(0.75)
    iqr = q3 - q1
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "IQR outliers": ((frame[num] < q1 - 1.5 * iqr) | (frame[num] > q3 + 1.5 * iqr)).sum(),
        "|z| > 3": ((frame[num] - frame[num].mean()) / frame[num].std()).abs().gt(3).sum(),
        "min": frame[num].min(), "max": frame[num].max(),
    }).round(2)

outlier_table(df)
Out[16]:

Neither rule flags a single value: every feature stays inside a sensible physical range (pH 4.8–8.2, moisture 8–65%, temperature 12–42 °C). The data is clean. That is worth knowing, but it doesn't show the rules working, so 40 typical sensor faults are injected into a copy (a stuck moisture probe reading 999, a temperature logged in Fahrenheit, a negative rainfall) to check that the rules catch them:

In [17]:
faulty = df.sample(50_000, random_state=0).reset_index(drop=True)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
bad = rng.choice(len(faulty), 40, replace=False)
faulty.loc[bad[:15], "Soil_Moisture"] = 999.0
faulty.loc[bad[15:30], "Temperature_C"] = faulty.loc[bad[15:30], "Temperature_C"] * 9 / 5 + 32
faulty.loc[bad[30:], "Rainfall_mm"] = -faulty.loc[bad[30:], "Rainfall_mm"]

table = outlier_table(faulty)
q1, q3 = faulty[num].quantile(0.25), faulty[num].quantile(0.75)
flag = ((faulty[num] < q1 - 1.5 * (q3 - q1)) | (faulty[num] > q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1))).any(axis=1)
print(f"rows flagged by the IQR rule: {flag.sum()} · injected faults caught: {flag[bad].sum()} of 40")
table.loc[["Soil_Moisture", "Temperature_C", "Rainfall_mm"]]

rows flagged by the IQR rule: 36 · injected faults caught: 36 of 40
Out[17]:
IQR outliers |z| > 3 min max
Soil_Moisture 15 15 8.01 999.00
Temperature_C 13 15 12.00 105.24
Rainfall_mm 8 9 -2479.97 2499.69

Both rules catch most of the faults: the z-score rule flags 39 of the 40 bad values and the IQR rule 36. For flat, uniform-like features the IQR fences end up further from the data than three standard deviations do (for a uniform feature, 1.5 IQR beyond the quartiles is wider than 3 sd from the mean), so the IQR rule is the more cautious of the two here. The misses are values that land close to the normal range, such as a cool morning logged in Fahrenheit (about 55 °F) or a small negative rainfall. Single-feature rules can't see those, which is why CSE274 uses multivariate detectors such as Isolation Forest.

C. Trends¶

A trend is a steady change along an ordered variable. Mean need climbs with temperature in a clean, almost linear way, and falls with soil moisture:

In [18]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
for ax, col in zip(axes, ["Temperature_C", "Soil_Moisture"]):
    bins = pd.cut(df[col], 25)
    m = s2.groupby(bins, observed=True)["need"].agg(["mean", "sem"])
    x = [b.mid for b in m.index]
    ax.errorbar(x, m["mean"], yerr=1.96 * m["sem"], fmt="o-", ms=4, color=plotting.ACCENT, capsize=2)
    ax.set(xlabel=col.replace("_", " "), ylabel="mean need score")
axes[0].set_title("Rising with temperature")
axes[1].set_title("Falling with soil moisture")
fig.tight_layout()
plotting.save("g03-trends")
plt.show()

8. EDA workflow integration¶

What this notebook decided for the modelling work:

Finding Consequence
No missing values, no duplicates no imputation needed
High is 3.3% of rows stratified splits; optimise balanced accuracy; class weights or resampling
Moisture, temperature, rainfall, wind, growth stage and mulching carry the signal candidates for engineered features (e.g. dryness = temperature / moisture)
Stage × mulching interaction tree models capture it for free; linear models need an interaction feature
Features are independent (VIF ≈ 1) linear-model coefficients are trustworthy
Distributions are bounded and not heavy-tailed scaling is safe; outlier removal not needed

The loop is: inspect → visualise one variable → visualise pairs → quantify (correlation, skew) → check for anomalies → write down decisions. The next notebooks use every one of these decisions.
